title: Judging statistical claims
log: 2026-11-12T12:44:20Z match: Claude Haiku 5.5 found no bank point the same, so it is written new

match.reason: The closest bank card, mat-questioning-statistical-claims, covers bias, sample size and correlation versus cause but not checking how a graph is displayed, which the brief asks for, and the Victorian card that does cover graph axes is written for Units 3 and 4, not Year 10.

draft.title: Judging statistical claims
card: a claim about a large group is only as good as the sample behind it. A small sample, or one that leaves out some of the group, can give a biased result.
a sample is biased when it favours some people over others. A survey about school lunches given only to students in the canteen queue is biased.
check the graph as well as the data. An axis that starts well above zero can make a small difference look large.
two things that rise and fall together are correlated. That does not show one causes the other, as a third factor may drive both.
draft.remember: Ask who was sampled, how it is shown, and whether a link is really a cause.

a.q: A poll asks 20 people leaving a gym whether Australians exercise enough. It reports that most Australians exercise enough. What is the main problem?
opts: The sample is small and biased
a.why: Gym visitors are more likely to exercise, and 20 people is few, so the sample does not represent all Australians. Asking about exercise is not itself a problem.
a.clue: Who is more likely to be outside a gym?

b.q: A town finds that in summer, ice cream sales and shark sightings both rise. A paper claims ice cream causes shark sightings. What is the best response?
opts: Correlation alone does not show cause
The claim is right, as both rise together
Sharks are drawn by the ice cream
The claim is right if sales are high enough
b.why: Both rise together, but that does not show one causes the other. Warm weather brings more swimmers and more ice cream buyers, so a third factor likely drives both. A stronger link would not prove cause alone.
b.clue: Could something else make both rise in summer?

a.best: The sample is small and biased

b.best: Correlation alone does not show cause
